Tito’s has remained virtually unchanged since it opened back in 1984. While the Westside is a culinary wonderland, there is simply nothing else on the Westside right now close to three tacos for less than $6. If you are after an Instagram type foodie moment, Tito’s is not the obvious choice. But, if you’re feeling nostalgic or just simply looking for something to fill the stomach, Tito’s is it.

Social enterprises are an eclectic mix of services offering to do charitable work in a business sense or to offer a socially conscious commercial objective. How does Knight's problem affect you?
Despite Sarkar's cynicism, the Knight event does indeed affect individual investors at least three ways.
Understanding what went on and what came next will take your sense of control over your own portfolio to an entirely new level.
Lesson #2: Where's the Insurance?
You couldn't see the Knight collapse coming, but that's not surprising. Unlike any other time in recent memory, no self-respecting individual investor ever got over the feeling that they had lost their bearings in the market. Because the Fed had, basically, built an anti-gravity device to keep stocks levitated in the air, individual investors didn't really have a clue about how stocks and stock markets worked. As such, proactive money management was about non-existent.
When Knight crashed and, presumably, key employees at other major brokerage houses did their best to keep from crashing, that really put a halt to any notion that the game would come back. Morgan Stanley announced on Aug. 3 that it would close out trading for the day. So did ICAP, a financial contracts broker, which took care of about 1% of Knight's trades. The following day, the New York Stock Exchange halted trading in all new stock issues. Other major financial hubs, including Chicago and London, suspended trading for the day as well.
What should have rightfully sounded three alarms for investors did no such thing. On Aug. 2, what was reported widely as "Failure Syndrome" came out of the woodwork to explain this entire Knight disaster.
To humor the alarms, we assume an arbitrary 10,000 stocks traded on U.S. exchanges, roughly 25% of which are accredited users of Knight's services. So we need to triple our 10,000 to approximate the entire likely universe of stocks blown to and fro on the Knight catastrophe. That in a nutshell is FS, or the Failure Syndrome.
Knight failed not because of a default, a computer glitch, or bad loans
